statements.text: As AI systems increasingly impact many areas of our lives, we deserve to know when AI is behind what we see and what decisions are being made about us. Transparency is essential for public trust in information and institutions that are using AI.For high-risk use cases, we also need to understand—in detail—how AI systems actually work and how to correct errors.
statements.venue: Remarks at Senate AI Insight Forum on transparency

statements.text: The challenge is that many of the most successful AI architectures developed in these last few years are, by design, too complicated for humans to make sense of.So we need to make progress in two directions: First, building tools that help humans interpret the decisions made by these complex AI systems. Second, supporting research into alternative AI architectures that are more interpretable or controllable by design.
statements.venue: Remarks at Senate AI Insight Forum on transparency

statements.text: As the Founder and Co-Chair of the Senate's bipartisan AI Caucus and a member of Majority Leader Chuck Schumer's bipartisan AI working group, I'm committed to developing smart policy that invests in American innovation and delivers the benefits of AI, while also establishing guardrails to protect against AI's risks.
statements.venue: Senator's website issue page on AI

statements.text: As an engineer, I appreciate the value of emerging technologies, but I am also mindful of the challenges they present. As lawmakers, we have the critical responsibility of ensuring a careful balance between mitigating the risks of new technologies like AI and fostering its tremendous economic and national security benefits.
statements.venue: Senate press release on the American AI Initiative executive order

statements.text: I am proud to announce the formation of the bipartisan AI Caucus in the Senate with Senator Rob Portman. Together, we will work with our colleagues to develop smart policy in a responsible way to ensure the United States remains at the forefront of innovation while maintaining important ethical, safety, and privacy standards.
statements.venue: Senate press release launching the Senate AI Caucus

statements.text: As you know our Nation is at a critical juncture in advancing precision agriculture technology and related artificial intelligence. To ensure producers have access to safe digital tools to guide and enhance management and production options, Congress provided US Department of Agriculture (UDSA) Agriculture Research Service with the initial planning funding to co-locate and establish a national center for resilient and regenerative precision agriculture in Lincoln at the Nebraska Innovation Campus. This facility is envisioned to serve as the anchor of a national network comprised of USDA and land-grant universities and their Cooperative Extension arms to equip America's farmers and ranchers with 21st century precision technologies to meet present-day and future challenges.
statements.context: Written question submitted by Senator Deb Fischer to Secretary Vilsack for the FY2024 Agriculture, Rural Development, FDA, and Related Agencies appropriations hearing record.

statements.text: Do you think that Meta's AI and Trust Safety Team, or for that matter the team for any AI developer, have the capability to really understand what the potential risks and benefits are? To be able to know whether or not making a system, putting into the wild, or making it open is a good idea?
statements.context: Senator Heinrich poses a final question to Dr. Yann LeCun during an open Senate hearing on the national security implications of AI.

statements.text: I know Microsoft recently reported that PRC influence campaigns on social media are increasingly leveraging generative AI technologies to create content for those operations, which allows them to create deceptive content much more quickly, much more effectively, and to spread that content. For any of you, talk about what you're seeing on this front from your perspective?
statements.context: Senator Heinrich poses a question during an open Senate hearing on countering China's malign influence operations in the United States.

statements.text: President Biden's Executive Order is the single most significant and substantive action taken by any government to date to govern AI based on democratic principles. The President is right to commit American leadership and expertise to the task of ensuring cutting-edge AI systems are developed and deployed responsibly.
statements.venue: Senate press release on Biden AI executive order

statements.text: This Executive Order applies the full scope of the administration's authorities in this area, but ultimately Congress is going to have to legislate. Congress must proactively lead on responsible AI development, using this Executive Order as a baseline. We need to invest in American innovation that can lead to major benefits, and we need to establish sufficient guardrails to minimize AI's risks.
statements.venue: Senate press release on Biden AI executive order

statements.text: It would be unwise to treat AI the way we did the internet and social media early on, and say, 'Oh, we can wait until later to implement some guardrails,' [...] This is very fast-moving technology, and the opportunities for great things are enormous, but the opportunities for abuse are also substantial.
statements.venue: TIME 100 Most Influential People in AI profile, reposted on Senate site

statements.text: Question. Commissioner Califf, artificial intelligence (AI) is dramatically impacting every aspect of our lives, including the field of drug development, and it is critical that the FDA is prepared to address AI-related issues in a systematic way.
statements.context: Senate Appropriations subcommittee hearing on the FY2025 Agriculture/FDA budget, written Q&A between Senator Heinrich and FDA Commissioner Califf.

statements.text: the President's executive order on AI has unleashed a whole swath of activity across agencies [...]
statements.context: Senate Appropriations subcommittee hearing on Energy and Water Development for FY2025, with Senator Heinrich questioning Energy Secretary Granholm on DOE AI initiatives.

statements.text: In the midst of rapid AI advancements, the Senate can lead or be led. We plan to lead, to deliver for the American people, helping ensure that AI comes as a benefit to society, not a threat,
statements.venue: Press release on bipartisan AI roadmap (Schumer site)

statements.text: when we look at how to deal with the $100,000 a second and how we make the 19-18 percent of GDP on health care trim down, and not just GLP-1 but many other ways that we think are using technology and AI and better management to manage health care in America.
statements.context: Senator Martin Heinrich speaking at a hearing on AI's potential to fuel economic growth and improve governance.

statements.text: For me, that is maybe the most exciting part of AI. Not ChatGPT-4, 5 or 6 or 7, but the notion that everything from fusion energy to how our biology works, etcetera, etcetera, that you can use machine learning, the predictive parts of AI to figure things out.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on AI's potential to fuel economic growth and improve governance, featuring testimony from a Sandia National Laboratories scientist.

statements.text: We heard a little bit about the importance of labor and workforce in having, maintaining our advantages in AI. But you mentioned something else, which is data. Talk a little bit about what the unique data sets that we have at places like our national labs, within our agencies, and how some of that—and for that matter data curation, the importance of data curation, how that gives us a leg up over some of our competitors as well.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI's potential to fuel economic growth and improve governance, chaired by Senator Heinrich.

statements.text: That when we did that, all we were doing was essentially embracing anti-competitiveness, and locking in the advantage of the incumbents. We need to be very careful about that.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI's potential to fuel economic growth and improve governance, chaired by Senator Heinrich.

statements.text: You have often said that artificial intelligence is the Manhattan Project of our time. And yet, this budget proposes a 14 percent cut to the Office of Science and a 57 percent cut to ARPA-E, where our major AI R&D efforts are currently underway.
statements.context: Senate hearing on the President's FY 2026 DOE budget request, during Senator Heinrich's opening remarks.

statements.text: I am going to shift gears to AI for a moment. A number of us announced a new AI roadmap today, and NIST is a big part of that; the Safety Institute at NIST in particular. How do we make sure that the AI Safety Institute at NIST is also leveraging the capacity that exists in other parts of the Federal Government?
statements.context: Senate Appropriations subcommittee hearing on Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies funding for FY2025, featuring Secretary Raimondo.
